lesson.body:
Here's a wine word worth knowing: tannin. It's not a flavor you taste, it's a feeling you notice. Tannin is that drying, grippy sensation that makes your gums and the insides of your cheeks feel a little rough or sticky, almost like your mouth has been wiped dry. The closest everyday example is a cup of black tea you left to steep too long — that puckery grip on your tongue is tannin at work. You'll meet it mostly in red wines.

So where does it come from? Tannin lives in the parts of the grape you don't eat much of: the skins, seeds, and stems. Reds get their color and their grip by soaking with those skins, which is why they're grippier than whites. Aging wine in oak barrels can add tannin too.

A little tannin gives a wine structure and backbone. Two things tame it: time and food. Tannins soften as a wine ages over years, and fatty or protein-rich foods — think steak or cheese — smooth that grip beautifully. That's why bold reds and a juicy burger are such good friends.
outcomes: Recognise tannin as a dry, grippy feeling
Choose food for a tannic red

deep_notes: Tannins belong to a family of natural compounds called polyphenols. They grab onto the proteins in your saliva, which normally keep your mouth slippery. Without that slick layer, your gums and cheeks feel rough and dry. The pros call this drying sensation astringency. They describe tannin by amount, from low to high, and by texture: fine, silky tannin feels smooth, while coarse tannin feels rough, a little like sandpaper.

Seed and stem tannins tend to be harsher and greener than skin tannins, so winemakers press gently to avoid crushing the seeds, and most remove the stems before fermenting. Some deliberately keep whole bunches, stems and all, for extra structure and a fresh, herbal edge. The longer the juice soaks with the skins, a step called maceration, the more tannin it usually pulls out. Most of the colour, by contrast, comes out in the first few days.

In a young wine, tannin feels firm and grippy. Over years in bottle, tannins slowly link up into larger chains that feel softer, and some drop out as sediment, the dark grit found in old bottles. Food works much faster. Proteins in meat or cheese bind to tannin before it can dry out your mouth, and fat coats your mouth, so the wine feels smoother.

deeper.body: Tannin is more than texture. It is a natural antioxidant, which means it slows down the damage oxygen does to wine. That is one reason firmly tannic reds, such as Barolo made from Nebbiolo or top Bordeaux, can keep improving in bottle for decades. Most light, low-tannin reds are best drunk young. Acidity and fruit help a wine age too.
deeper.title: Tannin helps wine age

v2.body:
For centuries, **tanners** turned animal hides into leather by soaking them in water with crushed oak bark. Something in the bark latched on to the proteins in the skin and toughened it. It was named after the trade: **tannin**, from the French word tan, crushed oak bark. The same kind of natural substance is in wine, and in a small way it grabs your mouth too.

Tannin is a feeling, not a flavour. It is the drying sensation on your gums, your tongue and the insides of your cheeks, as if your mouth had been wiped dry. The closest everyday example is black tea left to steep too long. You meet it mostly in red wines. **Acidity**, the sourness of lemons, does the opposite: it makes your mouth water.

Why dry? Tannins are natural plant substances that grab the proteins in your saliva (spit), which normally keep your mouth slippery. Without that slick layer, your mouth feels rough. Tasters call this drying feel **astringency**. Bite into unripe fruit and you get the same furry dryness.

Tannin sits in the solid parts of the grape: the skins, the seeds (the pips) and the stems. The juice has almost none. Oak barrels can add a little more, because the wood has tannin of its own, and new barrels give the most. Red wine ferments, meaning yeast turns its sugar into alcohol, with the skins in the juice. This **skin soak** gives it its colour and its tannin. The longer the soak, the more tannin. White wine is usually pressed (squeezed) off its skins first, so it has little. **Orange wine**, white grapes left on their skins, picks up some.

Grapes differ too. Thick-skinned grapes usually give more tannin.
• Pinot Noir: thin skins, low tannin
• Merlot: medium tannin
• Cabernet Sauvignon: thick skins, high tannin
• Nebbiolo, the grape of Barolo, a famous Italian red: pale wines with some of the firmest tannin in the world

Tasters judge tannin by amount, from low to high, and by texture. **Fine** tannin feels smooth, like silk or velvet; **coarse** tannin feels rough, like sandpaper. To find it, sip, swallow, then run your tongue along your gums. The drier they feel, the more tannin.

A little tannin gives a wine structure, like a backbone. Two things tame it: time and food. Over years in bottle, tannins slowly join into larger chains that feel softer, and some fall out as **sediment**, the dark grit in old bottles. Food works faster: the protein in steak or cheese grabs the tannin before it dries your mouth, and fat coats your mouth, so the wine feels smoother. That's why a bold red and a juicy burger are such good friends.
deep_notes: Tanning with bark is still done today and is called vegetable tanning. Hides are soaked in vats of ever stronger tannin, which binds to collagen, the main protein in skin, and coats it, so the leather resists water and rot. Oak bark was a classic source in Europe, alongside chestnut and other trees. The tannins in grapes are cousins of these bark tannins, which is why the old trade lent the wine world its word.

Tannin is not only in wine. For many people, tea and coffee are the main sources in their diet, and tannin is also found in many berries, in nuts and in dark chocolate. In wine, tasters treat it as part of the structure rather than the flavour, alongside acidity, alcohol and body. A red with no tannin at all can feel thin; with too much, it feels harsh and drying.

Scientists class astringency as a touch sensation, not one of the five tastes (sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, a savoury taste). Tannin clings most to a group of saliva proteins called proline-rich proteins. Once they clump together, saliva loses its slippery quality, so your mouth feels rough as your tongue moves. Tannin can also taste slightly bitter, but that is a separate thing: the dryness is the clue that tells you it is there.

Seed and stem tannins tend to be harsher and greener than skin tannins, so winemakers press gently to avoid crushing the seeds, and most remove the stems before fermenting. Some deliberately keep whole bunches, stems and all, for extra structure and a fresh, herbal edge. Ripeness matters too: in unripe grapes the seeds are green and the tannin harsh, while riper grapes, with brown seeds, give softer tannin.

Colour leaves the skins quickly, mostly in the first few days, while tannin keeps coming as the soak goes on. Warmth speeds this up. Grape skins float to the top of the tank as a thick layer called the cap. Winemakers push it down into the juice, or pump juice over it, to keep pulling out colour and tannin. Soaking too long or too hard can make tannin harsh, so the soak is judged carefully.

Cabernet Sauvignon has small berries with thick skins and lots of seed for little flesh, which is why it gives so much tannin. Merlot has thinner skins and less tannin, one reason winemakers in Bordeaux, in France, blend soft Merlot with sterner Cabernet. Pinot Noir's thin skins make pale wines with little tannin. Nebbiolo is the twist: light in colour, yet its young wines can be so drying that a traditional Barolo can need a decade or more to soften.

Fine and coarse describe the grain of tannin, much like fabric: silk and velvet at one end, sandpaper and felt at the other. Ripe grapes and gentle winemaking tend to give finer tannin; unripe grapes and soaking the skins too hard, coarser. A wine can be high in tannin yet feel polished. That is why tasters always describe both the amount and the texture, rather than just saying a wine is tannic.

In a young wine, tannin feels firm and drying. Over years in bottle, tannins slowly join with each other and with colour into larger chains that feel softer, until some become too large to stay in the wine and drop out as sediment. To leave that grit behind, an old red can be poured slowly into a glass jug called a decanter, stopping when the dark sludge reaches the neck of the bottle.

Fats and proteins reduce how strongly you feel tannin, so the wine's fruit seems to come forward. Proteins in meat or cheese bind to tannin before it can reach your saliva, and fat coats your mouth. That is why big, drying reds such as Cabernet Sauvignon are classic with steak, and young Barolo with rich meat dishes. A red with little tannin, like Pinot Noir, needs far less help and suits lighter food.

deeper.body: Tannin is more than texture. It is a natural antioxidant, which means it slows down the damage oxygen does to wine. That is one reason reds with firm tannin, such as Barolo made from Nebbiolo or top red Bordeaux, can keep improving in bottle for decades. Most light reds with little tannin are best drunk young. Acidity (sourness) and fruit help a wine age too.
